method: The basic rating life is the life that 90 % of a large group of apparently identical bearings reach or exceed before the first signs of fatigue, at constant load and speed on good-quality steel with conventional lubrication. ISO 281 expresses it in millions of revolutions as L10 = (C/P)^p, where C is the basic dynamic load rating from the bearing catalogue, P is the equivalent dynamic bearing load — the single constant load that produces the same fatigue as the actual combined radial and axial loading — and p is the life exponent, 3 for ball bearings and 10/3 for roller bearings. To read the same life in operating hours at a constant speed n in rpm, multiply by the 10^6 revolutions in a million and divide by the 60 n revolutions each hour makes: L10h = (10^6 / (60 n)) · (C/P)^p, the form in which catalogues usually tabulate the result. Because the exponent exceeds one, life grows faster than the rating: doubling C multiplies L10 by 2^p, eight times for a ball bearing, while doubling P divides it by the same factor. C is accepted from 0.001 to 1000000 kN, P from 0.001 to 1000000 kN, the speed from 0.001 to 1000000 rpm, and the type must be a ball or a roller bearing; results are rounded to six decimal places. When the equivalent load reaches half of the basic dynamic rating or more the page raises a caution, because ISO 281 warns that the life equation is not validated in that region and that the static load rating C0 and the bearing's minimum load then govern the selection. The basic life ignores the modified rating life, which adjusts for lubrication, contamination, the fatigue load limit and reliabilities other than 90 %, and it assumes the load and speed are steady. It is a preliminary engineering estimate, not a design review or a guarantee of service life. Everything runs locally in the browser with no storage, uploads or network access.
